title: Every Number Your Body Hits in One Day

scenes.say: Today, your body will build about three hundred and thirty billion brand new cells. That's almost four million every second. Including the second you just heard.
Since this video started, millions of your cells have already died, and been replaced. And that's just one of the numbers your body hits today.

visual.label: new cells since you pressed play

scenes.say: So let's follow one ordinary day, from midnight to midnight, and count everything. Six chapters. One clock. And at the end, one number that changes how you see yourself.
Chapter one. Midnight. You're asleep, and the hardest working muscle you own is just getting started.
At about seventy beats a minute, your heart will beat around one hundred thousand times before tonight. No breaks. No days off.
And every one of those beats moves blood. Altogether, your heart pushes around seventy five hundred liters through your body in a single day. That's about two thousand gallons.
But here's the question nobody asks. Where does all that blood actually go? Because it needs roads. A lot of roads.

If you took every artery, vein and capillary in your body, and laid them end to end, they would stretch about sixty thousand miles. Enough to wrap around the Earth almost two and a half times. Inside one person. Inside you.

And most of that length isn't the big pipes you can feel in your wrist or your neck. It's capillaries. Vessels so thin that red blood cells squeeze through them almost single file. That's where the real work happens: oxygen out, waste in.
But all that blood would be useless without one thing. And you're doing it right now, every four or five seconds.
Chapter two. Six in the morning. You wake up, and take a breath you'll never remember.
The American Lung Association puts it at more than seventeen thousand breaths a day. That's over six million a year.

visual.label: breaths in one day
visual.note: 12 to 15 a minute · American Lung Association

scenes.say: Every day, you pull in more than two thousand gallons of air. And it travels through about fifteen hundred miles of airways. Branches, inside branches, inside branches.

visual.title: WHAT GOES IN
rows: of air breathed in, every day

scenes.say: Spread out, the inside of your lungs covers roughly the area of a tennis court. And an adult man's lungs hold about six liters of air. All of that, folded into your chest.

visual.title: FOLDED INSIDE YOU
rows: of air, an adult man's lungs

scenes.say: And your two lungs are not twins. The right one has three lobes. The left one has only two. Why? Because it has to leave room for your heart.

visual.title: NOT TWINS
rows: your left lung, making room for your heart

scenes.say: But here's the part that surprises most people. When you lose fat, where does it actually go?

In twenty fourteen, scientists Ruben Meerman and Andrew Brown did the math. Burn ten kilos of fat, and eight point four kilos of it leaves through your lungs, as carbon dioxide. The rest becomes water.

visual.title: BURN 10 KG OF FAT
visual.sub: where it goes · Meerman & Brown, BMJ 2014

scenes.say: So the main exit for fat isn't sweat, and it isn't the toilet. It's your breath. Every time you exhale, a little bit of what you ate is leaving as gas.
So your lungs handle the gas. But your blood also picks up waste all day long. And someone has to clean it.
Chapter three. Ten in the morning. Just below your ribs, on either side of your spine, two organs about the size of a fist are hard at work. Your kidneys.
In a single day, your kidneys filter about one hundred and fifty quarts of blood. That's roughly one hundred and forty liters.

visual.label: quarts of blood filtered a day

scenes.say: Quick question before we go on. Which moves more through you in a day: the air you breathe, or the blood your heart pumps? Think about it for a second.

visual.title:
AIR OR
BLOOD?
visual.sub: which moves more in a day?

scenes.say: Here's the answer: it's almost a tie. Put both next to the other numbers from today, and you can see the job. Thousands of liters of air and blood move through you. About a hundred and forty liters get filtered. And only one or two quarts leave as urine.
Do the math, and that means about ninety nine percent of what your kidneys filter goes straight back into your blood. They're not throwing water away. They're sorting it, over and over, all day.

visual.label: percent sent back into your blood

scenes.say: How? Each kidney is packed with about a million tiny filtering units, called nephrons. A million in each one.
And the red blood cells passing through? Each one lives for about a hundred and twenty days. Then it's retired, and replaced. The blood in you right now is not the blood you had last summer.

visual.label: days a red blood cell lives

scenes.say: But none of this happens by itself. Every beat, every breath, every filter, is run by one organ that weighs about three pounds.
Chapter four. Two in the afternoon. You're reading, talking, deciding. And your brain is running all of it.
Inside it are close to eighty six billion nerve cells. And they talk to each other with electricity.
The fastest nerve signals in your body travel at up to a hundred and twenty meters per second. That's about two hundred and seventy miles per hour.
And while your brain is busy, your eyes keep doing something you never notice.
You blink about fourteen to seventeen times a minute. Across a waking day, that's up to around sixteen thousand blinks. Each one sweeps your eyes clean. And your brain simply edits them out.

Why don't you see the darkness? Because your brain fills in the gaps. It stitches the moments before and after each blink together, so the world looks continuous. You've been watching an edited version of reality your whole life.
So your brain hides the blinks. But there's something else you lose all day, and you can find it on your pillow.
Chapter five. Five in the afternoon. Look at your hairbrush. Or your shoulders.
Dermatologists say it's normal to shed between fifty and a hundred hairs a day. Every single day. Most people never notice.

visual.label: hairs lost a day, and that's normal
visual.note: 50 to 100 a day · American Academy of Dermatology

scenes.say: Why so many? Because every hair on your head runs on its own clock. It grows for years, then it rests, and then it lets go, so a new hair can push through from the same root. Losing hair every day is part of how you keep it.

visual.title:
GROW. REST.
LET GO.
visual.sub: every hair, on its own schedule.

scenes.say: Your nails are growing too. Fingernails, about three and a half millimeters a month. Toenails? Less than half that speed. About one point six.
Add up a year, and that's about four centimeters of fingernail, and about two of toenail. Pushed out from the base, a tiny bit every day.
But the strangest thing your body does today is happening deep inside your bones. And by tonight, it will make you shorter.

scenes.chapter: The frame: 2 cm shorter by night
scenes.say: Chapter six. Nine at night. You're about to go to bed, and you are measurably shorter than you were this morning.

Researchers at the University of Manchester say we can be up to two centimeters taller in the morning than when we go to bed. All day, gravity squeezes the soft discs in your spine. At night, lying down, they recover.

visual.label: centimeters shorter by night
visual.note: up to 2 cm · University of Manchester, 2016

scenes.say: And your skeleton has changed far more than that. You were born with about two hundred and seventy bones. As an adult, you have around two hundred and six. Many of them fused together as you grew.

The plates of a baby's skull, for example, start out separate, so the head can grow. Over time, they join. Bone isn't a dead frame you're carrying around. It's living tissue, constantly torn down and rebuilt.
But here's the number that changes everything. According to the U.S. Surgeon General's report on bone health, most of your adult skeleton is replaced about every ten years.

visual.label: years to replace most of your skeleton

scenes.say: New blood every few months. New bone every decade. So what's actually staying the same?
Midnight again. One full day. Let's count it up.
About a hundred thousand heartbeats. More than seventeen thousand breaths. A hundred and fifty quarts of blood, cleaned.
Up to sixteen thousand blinks. Up to a hundred hairs, gone. And two centimeters of height, lost, and found again.
And the number we started with. About three hundred and thirty billion new cells, built today. Every single day, without asking you.
So the body that wakes up tomorrow is not exactly the one that went to sleep. It's rebuilt, a little, every day. Counted.
There's a whole playlist of these, called Your Body in Numbers. The next one is on your screen right now. See you there.
